**Visual Analysis:**

- **Affected part:** Whole plant
- **Key features:**
  - Central tomato plant(s) show severe, complete wilt — stems and foliage drooping downward dramatically
  - Leaves still appear green (not yellowed or necrotic) despite total collapse
  - Adjacent plants on both sides remain healthy and upright
  - Sudden/rapid onset pattern (neighbor plants unaffected)
  - Commercial field with black plastic mulch, staked tomatoes, sandy/warm-climate environment

**Reasoning through differentials:**

| Disease | Fit |
|---|---|
| **Bacterial_Wilt** | Sudden whole-plant wilt, green leaves, single-plant pattern — classic |
| **Southern_Bacterial_Wilt** | Same pathogen (Ralstonia solanacearum), warm southern climate — very similar |
| Verticillium_Wilt | More gradual, V-shaped yellowing first — doesn't fit |
| Phytophthora_Blight | Dark stem lesions, water-soaked — not visible here |
| Tomato_Spotted_Wilt_Virus | Bronzing, ring spots, tip dieback — not seen |
| Bacterial_Canker_And_Wilt | Usually shows pith discoloration, cankers — not evident |

The image is a textbook presentation of **sudden, complete, whole-plant wilt with green (non-chlorotic) leaves** in a single tomato plant, with healthy neighbors. This is the hallmark of vascular bacterial wilt caused by *Ralstonia solanacearum*. The field setting (warm/arid climate, black plastic mulch, sandy soil) is consistent with conditions favoring this pathogen.
